title: Keppra and Alcohol: Can You Drink on Levetiracetam?
excerpt: Can you drink on Keppra? How levetiracetam and alcohol interact, why the real risk is seizure control and lost sleep, mood effects, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Keppra? How levetiracetam and alcohol interact, why lost sleep and missed doses raise seizure risk, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Keppra (levetiracetam) does not react with alcohol the way some medicines do. It is not broken down by the liver enzymes that alcohol affects, and the two don't create a toxic by-product. But that is not the same as safe. Both Keppra and alcohol slow your brain down, so together they can make you much sleepier, dizzier, and less coordinated than either one alone. And the bigger risk is indirect: heavy drinking, a short night's sleep, a skipped or vomited dose, and the rebound hours after alcohol wears off can all lower your seizure threshold, which is the point at which your brain tips into a seizure. That is the opposite of what you take Keppra for.

**The quick rules:** Talk to your neurologist before you drink at all. If they say an occasional drink is fine for you, keep it to one or two, never binge, never skip or delay a Keppra dose to make room for alcohol, and protect your sleep that night. Don't drive after drinking on Keppra. If a seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes, happens again before the person recovers, or causes trouble breathing or an injury, call 911.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance about levetiracetam. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your seizure history, your dose, and your other medicines. **Talk to your doctor before drinking if** you take Keppra, Keppra XR, generic levetiracetam, or brivaracetam (Briviact). **Get help right away if** a seizure lasts more than 5 minutes, seizures come back to back, someone doesn't wake up normally afterward, has trouble breathing, or is hurt. Call 911 in an emergency. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US.

## How Keppra and Alcohol Interact: The Real Mechanism

Most seizure medicines either calm the brain's electrical signaling by blocking sodium channels or boost GABA, the brain's main "slow down" chemical. Keppra does something different. It attaches to a protein called **SV2A**, which sits on the tiny packets (vesicles) that nerve cells use to release chemical messages. By binding there, levetiracetam is thought to dampen the bursts of over-excited signaling that spread into a seizure. Researchers still don't fully understand every step, but the SV2A target is well established.

Alcohol works on the brain through other routes. In the short term it boosts GABA's calming effect and blocks glutamate, the brain's main "go" signal. That's why a few drinks make you relaxed, slow, and sleepy.

So the interaction comes down to three things.

### 1. Stacked sedation (the immediate effect)

Keppra and alcohol don't bind to the same targets, but they push the brain in the same direction. Keppra's most common side effects, according to its prescribing information, are **sleepiness, tiredness, weakness, and dizziness**. It can also affect coordination and balance, especially in the first weeks or after a dose increase. Alcohol does all of those things too. Put them together and you can end up more impaired than you expect from the number of drinks you had. That matters for falls, for driving, and for judging how much you've had.

### 2. Very little liver interaction (the reassuring part)

Here Keppra is unusual. Many seizure medicines, like carbamazepine and phenytoin, are heavily processed by liver enzymes, and drinking can shift their blood levels. Levetiracetam is different. Most of it leaves your body **unchanged in your urine**, cleared by the kidneys, and the portion that is broken down isn't handled by the cytochrome P450 liver enzymes that alcohol affects. That's why Keppra has relatively few drug interactions in general. It also means one drink is not going to push your Keppra levels up or down the way it might with some other drugs.

This is the reason some people read that Keppra "doesn't interact with alcohol." Chemically that's close to true. Practically, it misses the point.

### 3. Seizure threshold (the risk that actually matters)

The reason to be careful has less to do with Keppra and more to do with what alcohol does to a brain that's prone to seizures:

- **Rebound after drinking.** While alcohol is in your system it calms the brain. As it wears off, the brain swings the other way and becomes more excitable for a while. After heavy drinking, this rebound is when alcohol-related seizures tend to happen, usually somewhere between 6 and 48 hours after the last drink.
- **Lost sleep.** Sleep deprivation is one of the best-known seizure triggers. Alcohol makes you fall asleep faster but breaks up sleep in the second half of the night, so you get less deep, restful sleep than the hours in bed suggest. Our guide to [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains how that happens.
- **Missed or lost doses.** People forget evening doses after a night out, or skip them on purpose because they've been drinking. Vomiting soon after a dose can mean some of it never gets absorbed. Any of these drops your protection right when you need it most.
- **Dehydration and low blood sugar.** Heavy drinking can leave you dehydrated and, especially if you didn't eat, with low blood sugar. Both can add stress on a brain that's already near its threshold.

Put simply, the drinking itself, plus everything that tends to come with a big night, is what threatens seizure control. Keppra can't fully offset that.

## What the Label and Guidance Actually Say

It helps to separate what's documented from what's often repeated.

- **The US prescribing information** for Keppra lists sleepiness, fatigue, dizziness, and coordination problems among its main warnings, and advises patients not to drive or operate machinery until they know how the drug affects them. It also includes warnings about **behavior and mood changes**, including irritability, aggression, anxiety, depression, and, rarely, psychotic symptoms.
- **The patient leaflets used in the UK and Europe** go further on alcohol specifically. They advise that, as a safety precaution, you should not take Keppra with alcohol.
- **Like every antiepileptic drug,** levetiracetam carries an FDA warning about a small increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior. Alcohol is a depressant, which is one more reason to watch your mood if you combine them.
- **Epilepsy charities and specialists** generally say that many adults with well-controlled epilepsy can have small amounts of alcohol, but that heavy drinking and binge drinking clearly raise seizure risk, and that the decision should be made with your own doctor. Research on moderate drinking in people with epilepsy has generally not shown that one or two drinks set off seizures in most people, but the studies are small and individual risk varies a lot.

So the official picture is consistent: no dangerous chemical reaction, real added sedation, real mood cautions, and a seizure risk that rises steeply with how much you drink.

## Can You Drink on Keppra at All?

This is the question most people searching "Keppra and alcohol" actually want answered. The honest answer is: **it depends on you, and your neurologist is the right person to decide.** Things that usually make a doctor more cautious include:

- Your seizures aren't fully controlled yet, or you've had a seizure in recent months.
- You've just started Keppra or had a recent dose change, when side effects like drowsiness and mood changes are most common.
- You've had seizures in the past that were linked to drinking or to sleep loss.
- You take other medicines that also cause sleepiness, such as benzodiazepines, opioids, sleep aids, or other seizure medicines.
- You've noticed mood or behavior changes on Keppra.
- You drink heavily, or have trouble stopping once you start.

If your doctor does say occasional light drinking is acceptable, a few habits make it safer:

1. **Keep it small.** One or two standard drinks, spread out, with food. Avoid shots, drinking games, and anything that makes it hard to keep count.
2. **Take every dose on time.** Set an alarm for your evening dose before you go out. Don't skip a dose "because you've been drinking."
3. **Protect your sleep.** Plan a normal bedtime and a full night. A late night plus alcohol is a double hit to your seizure threshold.
4. **Tell someone you're with.** Make sure at least one person knows you have epilepsy and what to do if you have a seizure.
5. **Don't drive.** Even if you feel fine, the combination can slow your reactions more than you notice.

## Keppra and Alcohol Side Effects: What You Might Notice

Combining the two can bring out or intensify effects such as:

- Heavy drowsiness or trouble staying awake
- Dizziness, unsteadiness, or poor coordination
- Slowed thinking or trouble concentrating
- Blurred or double vision
- Irritability, anger, or a short temper
- Low mood, anxiety, or tearfulness the next day

The mood effects deserve special attention. Some people on levetiracetam notice irritability or anger, sometimes nicknamed "Keppra rage" in patient forums. Alcohol lowers inhibitions. Together they can lead to arguments or outbursts you wouldn't normally have, or a much darker mood the next day. If drinking on Keppra leaves you feeling angry, hopeless, or not like yourself, that's important information for your doctor. Don't just push through it.

## The Keppra Hangover: Why Mornings Can Feel Worse

A lot of people on Keppra report that hangovers hit harder than they used to. That makes sense even without any special interaction. Keppra's everyday side effects (tiredness, weakness, fogginess) overlap with hangover symptoms. Alcohol disrupts sleep. Mild dehydration and poor sleep make everything feel worse.

There's a more serious point here too. **The conditions that make a hangover miserable are the same ones that make a seizure more likely:** short, broken sleep, dehydration, an empty stomach, and the alcohol rebound. If you wake up badly hungover on Keppra:

- **Take your morning dose on time** with water and, if you can, something to eat.
- **If you vomited soon after an evening dose,** don't take an extra dose on your own. Call your pharmacist or doctor and ask what to do. Many seizure plans have specific advice for this.
- **Rest and rehydrate.** Water and some food matter more than any hangover remedy.
- **Skip the sedating hangover fixes.** Don't add antihistamine sleep aids or "PM" painkillers to sleep it off without asking a pharmacist. They stack with Keppra's drowsiness.
- **Take shakiness seriously.** Ordinary hangover shakes are common, and our guide to [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes) explains what's behind them. But jerking movements you can't control, staring spells, or confusion are different. If you have a seizure plan, follow it.

## How Long After Keppra Can You Drink?

This is a common search, and the answer surprises some people: **there's no window to wait for.** Keppra is a daily medicine meant to keep a steady level in your blood around the clock. Its half-life in healthy adults is roughly 6 to 8 hours, which is why the standard tablets are taken twice a day. You always take the next dose before the last one wears off.

That means:

- You can't "wait it out" before drinking the way you might with a one-off painkiller.
- You should **never skip or delay a dose** to create a gap for alcohol. A missed dose lowers your protection, and it's one of the most common causes of breakthrough seizures.
- If you're wondering how long the *alcohol* stays in your system, that's a separate question. The body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though that varies a lot. Our guide on [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) has the details.

## Keppra and Alcohol Withdrawal Seizures

Two different situations get mixed up here.

**If you take Keppra for epilepsy:** heavy drinking followed by stopping (for example, a weekend binge followed by a dry Monday) can trigger the brain's rebound period. In someone who already has a lower seizure threshold, that's a real risk window, even if they're taking Keppra faithfully.

**If you drink heavily every day:** stopping suddenly can cause alcohol withdrawal, which can include seizures whether or not you have epilepsy. That's a medical issue, and it should be handled with a doctor. Signs include shaking hands, sweating, a racing heart, anxiety, nausea, and in severe cases confusion or hallucinations. Keppra isn't a standard treatment for alcohol withdrawal and shouldn't be used to manage it on your own. If you drink most days and want to cut back, talk to your doctor first about the safest way to do it.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

Be especially cautious, and make sure you've talked to your prescriber, if you:

- Have seizures that aren't fully controlled
- Are newly started on Keppra or recently changed dose
- Take other sedating medicines, such as benzodiazepines like [Klonopin](/never-hungover/klonopin-and-alcohol), opioids, sleep aids, or [gabapentin](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol)
- Have kidney disease (Keppra is cleared by the kidneys, so doses are often adjusted)
- Have a history of depression, anxiety, or mood changes on Keppra
- Are pregnant or planning a pregnancy
- Are an older adult, since falls from combined dizziness can cause serious injury

For a wider look at how common medicines and supplements interact with alcohol, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## When to Get Help Right Away

> **Call 911 or go to the emergency room if:**
> - A seizure lasts **longer than 5 minutes**
> - A second seizure starts before the person has fully recovered from the first
> - The person has **trouble breathing**, turns blue, or doesn't wake up normally afterward
> - The person is injured, hit their head, or had the seizure in water
> - It's a **first-ever seizure**
> - Someone is very hard to wake after drinking on Keppra, has slow or irregular breathing, or is vomiting while drowsy
>
> **Call your doctor soon if:** you had a breakthrough seizure after drinking, you've been missing doses, drinking on Keppra leaves you unusually angry or depressed, or you're unsure whether to take a dose you might have vomited up. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, call or text **988** in the US.

If you're with someone having a seizure: keep them safe from hard or sharp objects, cushion their head, don't put anything in their mouth, don't hold them down, turn them on their side once the jerking stops, and time the seizure.

## Do Hangover Supplements Like DHM Help? Not on Keppra

If you're on Keppra, the most useful hangover strategy is keeping drinking light enough that there's little hangover to treat. That protects your sleep and your seizure control at the same time. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also use **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on the brain. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. One widely cited rat study suggested DHM acts on GABA-A receptors in the brain, which is part of why it's being studied. That's also exactly why anyone with epilepsy should **check with their neurologist or pharmacist before trying it.** There's no good research on how DHM interacts with levetiracetam or with seizure control, and no supplement makes it safer to drink on Keppra.

There's no hangover supplement we'd suggest for someone on Keppra. If you want to talk about anything at all, take the bottle to your neurologist or pharmacist and ask before the first dose. For the wider picture of how supplements and medicines interact, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## The Bottom Line

- Keppra (levetiracetam) has very little chemical interaction with alcohol, because it's mostly cleared by the kidneys rather than the liver.
- The two do stack up on **sleepiness, dizziness, and poor coordination**, and can worsen **irritability and low mood**.
- The real risk is to **seizure control**: heavy drinking, the rebound hours afterward, lost sleep, and missed or vomited doses can all lower your seizure threshold.
- There's no waiting period that makes drinking safe, and you should **never skip a dose** to drink.
- Ask your neurologist whether any alcohol is OK for you. If they say yes, keep it light, take every dose on time, sleep well, and don't drive.
- A seizure longer than 5 minutes, repeated seizures, or trouble breathing means calling 911.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Keppra?**

Some people with well-controlled epilepsy are told by their neurologist that an occasional drink or two is acceptable, but that decision belongs to your doctor, not a label or a website. Keppra (levetiracetam) and alcohol both cause drowsiness and dizziness, and the bigger danger is indirect: heavy drinking, lost sleep, missed doses, and the hours after drinking can all lower your seizure threshold. If you have not discussed alcohol with your prescriber, ask before you drink.

**Does alcohol make Keppra less effective?**

Alcohol does not appear to change how your body processes levetiracetam in any major way, because the drug is mostly cleared by the kidneys rather than the liver. The problem is that drinking can work against the medicine's job. Binge drinking, the rebound period as alcohol leaves your system, poor sleep, and forgotten or vomited doses can all make a seizure more likely even when Keppra levels are normal.

**How long after taking Keppra can I drink?**

There is no safe waiting window, because Keppra is taken every day and is meant to stay in your system all the time. Its half-life is roughly 6 to 8 hours in healthy adults, but you take the next dose before it wears off. Never skip or delay a dose to make room for drinking. Skipping is one of the most reliable ways to trigger a breakthrough seizure.

**Is levetiracetam the same as Keppra when it comes to alcohol?**

Yes. Levetiracetam is the generic name and Keppra is the original brand, along with the extended-release version (Keppra XR) and other generics. The same cautions apply to all of them. A related drug, brivaracetam (Briviact), works in a similar way, and its prescribing information notes that alcohol can add to its sedating effects, so the same caution applies.

**Why do I feel so hungover after drinking on Keppra?**

Keppra's most common side effects are sleepiness, tiredness, weakness, and dizziness, which overlap heavily with a hangover. Alcohol also fragments sleep in the second half of the night. Stack the two and the next day can feel much worse than the amount you drank suggests. A heavy hangover is also a warning sign, because the poor sleep and dehydration behind it are the same conditions that can make a seizure more likely.

**Can drinking on Keppra cause a seizure?**

It can make one more likely, especially after heavy drinking. Alcohol-related seizures most often happen in the hours after drinking stops, as the brain rebounds from alcohol's calming effect, typically 6 to 48 hours later. Sleep loss and missed doses add to that risk. A seizure that lasts longer than 5 minutes, repeated seizures, trouble breathing, or an injury during a seizure all need emergency care: call 911.

**Can Keppra and alcohol affect my mood?**

Yes, potentially. Keppra's label warns about behavior and mood changes such as irritability, aggression, anxiety, and depression, and all seizure medicines carry a warning about suicidal thoughts. Alcohol lowers inhibitions and is a depressant. If you notice anger, low mood, or dark thoughts after drinking on Keppra, stop drinking and tell your doctor. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US.

**Is it safe to take DHM or other hangover supplements with Keppra?**

Check with your neurologist or pharmacist first. There is no good research on how DHM, or most hangover supplements, interact with levetiracetam or with seizure control. DHM is thought to act on GABA receptors in the brain, which is one more reason to get a professional opinion before adding it if you have epilepsy. No supplement makes it safer to drink on Keppra.
